title: Two fountains (fourth rooms)
hookLine: one basin filled by pipes and effort, one filled from a spring beneath

cards: Two stone basins sit side by side in a garden. Both end up full of water. But the first is fed by a long line of pipes and channels from somewhere far away.
Somebody had to build all that, and somebody has to keep it working. You can hear the water clanking through. The second sits right on top of a spring.
Nobody pipes anything in. It just fills, from underneath, quietly, and keeps on filling. Teresa of Ávila says prayer can come both of these ways.
Today's word is the second one.

teach.h: THE FIRST BASIN: OUR OWN EFFORT.
teach.b: First, the pipes. The first basin, Teresa says, is like the good feelings that come from prayer by our own effort. We read, we think, we picture the Gospel scenes, we work at it.
And it does bring joy; that's real, and it's good. But it comes the long way, with noise, through our own pipes.

teach.h: THE SECOND: A SPRING FROM GOD.
teach.b: Second, the spring. In the second basin, the water rises from God, right at the source, and fills without anyone building anything. Teresa calls this the prayer of quiet.
The mind may still wander, but the will, the deepest part that loves, is held still and at peace with God.
The heart widens, she says, and she reaches for a psalm, in the Douay-Rheims: "I have run the way of thy commandments, when thou didst enlarge my heart."
Third, you can't force it. Here Teresa is very clear. You can't dig for this spring, or make it happen by trying harder.
It's a gift. What you can do, she says, is make room: be humble, keep praying, and don't cling to the feelings when they come or panic when they leave. Fourth, love over thinking.

teach.h: NOT TO THINK MUCH, BUT LOVE MUCH.
teach.b: In these rooms she writes a line short enough to carry: the important thing isn't to think much, but to love much. If the mind is racing, let it, like a mill clattering in the background.
The will can still rest by the spring. That's the difference between the two fountains. Not how much water.

how: In the Carmelite tradition, people who pray regularly are taught not to force feelings in prayer but to stay faithful and receptive, and spiritual directors use Teresa's two fountains to help them tell effort from gift.

o: a vow of silence kept by nuns in a Spanish convent
a quiet hour of reading the nuns kept after supper
Teresa's prayer of quiet, where the will rests in God

games.q: what's inside the fountains — tap the pairs.
p: filled by pipes: our own effort
filled from a spring: God's gift
a mill clattering in the background

s: you can bring on the prayer of quiet by trying harder
Teresa says it's a gift. you can make room for it, but you can't dig for the spring.
in the prayer of quiet, the mind may still wander
Teresa compares it to a clattering mill; the will can still rest in God.
Teresa says the good feelings from our own effort are worthless
she calls them real and good. they just come the long way, through the pipes.

games.q: you're sitting in prayer and a deep, quiet peace arrives. then your mind starts racing about tomorrow. what does Teresa say to do?
o: stop praying until your mind is calm.
let the mind clatter, and let the heart keep resting.
fight every thought until it's gone.
games.why: she says the mind can be like a noisy mill while the will stays at rest with God. don't chase the noise.

practice: Don't try to produce any thought or feeling; picture yourself as a basin, with the spring underneath.

If you pray, stay with God without words, the way you'd sit beside someone you love without needing to talk; if you don't, let the stillness fill up on its own. When your mind clatters like a mill, let it clatter.

wordCard.voice: Quietud. Teresa's Spanish name for prayer that rises like a spring in the fourth rooms, a gift from God where the heart rests even as the mind wanders. Today's word.

orig.note: Spanish: prayer of quiet, Teresa's name for the prayer of the fourth rooms.

carryVoice: Your line: the spring beneath. Some water can't be pumped, only received. See you in the fifth rooms.
